latency.def: How long one request takes, from the moment it's sent to the moment the answer arrives. Usually measured in milliseconds.

throughput.def: How many requests (or how much data) a system handles per second. A system can have high throughput and still be slow for each request.

percentile.def: p99 is the time that 99% of requests beat; only the slowest 1% take longer. p50 is the median. Percentiles show the slow requests that averages hide.

availability.def: The share of time (or of requests) a system works and answers correctly, often quoted in 'nines': 99.9% allows about 8.8 hours of downtime a year.

durability.def: The promise that data the system has accepted won't be lost later, even when disks or machines fail.

eventual-consistency.def: Copies of the data may briefly disagree after a write, but catch up if no new writes arrive. Readers can see slightly old data for a moment.

redundancy.def: Keeping spare copies of a component or of data, so that when one fails another can take over.

error-budget.def: The failures a service is allowed under its availability target. 99.9% leaves a 0.1% budget; teams spend it on shipping changes and slow down when it runs out.

read-heavy.def: A system where reads far outnumber writes, like a link shortener that's opened far more often than links are created. Designs for these focus on making reads cheap.

redirect.def: A response that tells the browser to go to a different URL instead. 301 means 'moved for good' (browsers remember it); 302 means 'go there this time'.

cache.def: A fast store, usually in memory, that keeps copies of data that's read often, so it doesn't have to be fetched from the slower original every time.

load-balancer.def: A component that receives incoming requests and spreads them across several servers, skipping any that are unhealthy.

replica.def: A copy of a database kept up to date from the main one. Replicas can serve reads and take over if the main copy fails.

sharding.def: Splitting one large dataset across several databases (shards), each holding part of the data, so no single machine has to store or serve all of it.

message-queue.def: A buffer between programs: one side drops messages in, the other takes them out and processes them later, at its own pace.

cdn.def: Content delivery network: servers spread around the world that keep copies of files close to users, so they load faster.

ssd.def: Solid-state drive: storage built from memory chips instead of spinning platters. Much faster than a hard disk, much slower than RAM.

api.def: The set of requests a program accepts from other programs, and what it sends back. For a web service, usually its URLs and their inputs and outputs.

uuid.def: A 128-bit random-looking ID, usually written as 36 characters, that can be generated anywhere without checking with anyone and still be unique.

single-point-of-failure.def: One part whose failure takes the whole system down with it, because nothing else can do its job.

vertical-scaling.def: Handling more load by moving to a bigger machine: more CPU, memory or faster disks. No code changes, but there's a ceiling.

horizontal-scaling.def: Handling more load by adding more machines and spreading the work across them.

failover.def: Switching to a standby copy when the main one fails, so the system keeps working.

stateless.def: A server that keeps nothing between requests that another server would need, so any copy can handle any request.

sticky-session.def: A load balancer setting that always sends the same user to the same server. A workaround for servers that keep state.

health-check.def: A small request a load balancer sends to each server every few seconds. Servers that fail it stop getting traffic.

replication-lag.def: The delay between a write on the primary database and a replica applying it. During it, the replica returns old data.

hit-rate.def: The share of reads a cache answers itself. The rest (misses) go to the slower store behind it.

cache-aside.def: The app checks the cache first; on a miss it reads the database and stores the answer in the cache for next time.

ttl.def: Time to live: how long a cached copy may be kept before it expires and has to be fetched again.

origin.def: The servers that hold the real content behind a CDN. Edge servers fetch from the origin when they don't have a copy.

edge-server.def: One of a CDN's servers, placed close to users, that keeps copies of content so requests don't have to travel to the origin.

worker.def: A background program that takes jobs off a queue and does them, away from the requests users are waiting on.

at-least-once.def: A queue guarantee that every message is delivered, possibly more than once. Consumers must be safe to run twice.

idempotent.def: Safe to repeat: doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once, like setting a value rather than adding to it.

dead-letter-queue.def: A side queue for messages that keep failing, so they can be inspected without blocking the rest.
